reason: The trap here is the comma, and the verifier walked round it correctly. I confirmed the early reading independently: Representative Poetry Online, copy text Observations (The Dial Press, 1924), pp. 30 to 31, prints I too, dislike it: there are things that are important beyond all this fiddle., with one comma and a colon, so the proposal’s wording could never have belonged to 1919 or 1924. For the named edition I could not reach a scan of the 1967 book, but every independent account of Moore’s revision I checked gives the three line Complete Poems text as I, too, dislike it. / Reading it, however, with a perfect contempt for it, one discovers in / it, after all, a place for the genuine. Two commas, closing full stop, and line 1 is the whole of the first line, so the locator is exact and no slash is needed. The joint Macmillan and Viking imprint of 1967 is right, and the long version does sit in that book’s back matter, which is why the short text is the book’s poem and not an excerpt from it. Clear on the mechanical checks: shipped.js gives no exact hit, no near hit, Moore at zero for the year, not banned; 1967 is in scope; the tag Poetry is the form of the work; the source line is 75 characters, leads with the name, carries no dash and no straight quote. Two things I would fix before it ships, neither of them a refutation. First, the book is The Complete Poems of Marianne Moore, and the fuller title still fits inside 140 characters, so I have put it in betterCitation. Second, the note should say in one clause that the poem does not stop there: the sentence turns on however and ends at a place for the genuine. Line 1 alone is a famous piece of candour and squarely June’s plain speech, but a reader who meets only the four words can take Moore to be dismissing poetry when she is doing the reverse, and the note is the only place to say so. I flag it rather than refute because the citation itself is sound and rule 2 expressly blesses an opening line.
